Lesson 1 — Symmetry All Around Us (Anchoring Phenomenon + Lines of Symmetry):
Learners observe the anchoring phenomenon (the matatu conductor's mirror and the lorry's image) and the maize leaf. In pairs they fold paper cut-outs (equilateral triangle, rectangle, square, the letters A and F, a matatu outline) to find lines of symmetry, then build a class definition and test it on the Kenya flag. They open the Driving Question Board with their own questions and draw an Initial Model of what a mirror does to a shape.

Lesson 2 — Reflection All Around Us (Locating Lines of Symmetry with a Mirror):
Learners predict, then use a plane mirror and paper-folding on a maize leaf, a bottle cap, a rhombus, a regular hexagon and Maasai beadwork and kikoi patterns. They agree that a line of symmetry is a mirror line and that the two halves are congruent, add the mirror line to their Unit Model and update the Driving Question Board.

Lesson 3 — Reflection on the Cartesian Plane (Coordinate Rules):
Learners reflect a lorry-shaped quadrilateral ABCD in the y-axis, the x-axis, y = x and y = -x by counting grid squares, notice that each image point is as far from the mirror line as its object point and that the joining line meets the mirror line at a right angle, and write a coordinate rule for each mirror line on a Reference Card. They see that the distances between vertices do not change. The Driving Question Board and the model gain coordinate evidence; the sentence 'the image and object are ___' is left blank on purpose.

Lesson 4 — Properties of Reflection (Physical Investigation):
Using a plane mirror, a ruler, a set square and tracing paper, groups measure and verify the four properties of reflection: (I) the image is the same size as the object; (II) object and image are equidistant from the mirror line; (III) the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of every object-image segment; (IV) the image is laterally inverted. The tracing-paper fold lets learners name the image 'congruent' to the object and fill the blank left in Lesson 3. The Driving Question Board and the model are updated with the four properties.

Lesson 5 — Finding the Equation of the Mirror Line:
Given an object point and its image, learners work backwards: midpoint, gradient of the object-image segment, negative reciprocal, then the equation (P(2, 1) to P'(6, 5) gives y = -x + 7; A(-1, 4) to A'(3, 0) gives y = x + 1). They write a three-step Mirror Line Algorithm and meet the special cases of horizontal and vertical object-image segments. The Driving Question Board gains 'We can work backwards to find the mirror'.

Lesson 6 — Constructing Reflected Images (Drawing the Image on Plain Paper):
Learners construct the image of a Kenya flag outline and of an irregular plot of land near Kericho with ruler and set square, measure corresponding sides and see that all lengths are preserved, and write 'the image is congruent to the object'. They end with the question: what is the least information that proves two triangles congruent?

Lesson 7 — Congruence Tests for Triangles (SSS, SAS, AAS/ASA, RHS):
Learners construct triangles from partial information, find that each test fixes exactly one triangle (up to a flip), and meet direct and opposite congruence. They show that a reflected triangle is congruent to its object by SSS and that the congruence is opposite, which is why the lorry's image is a perfect copy that appears flipped. Kenyan context: identical roof trusses and tiles.

Lesson 8 — Final Explanation (Model Revision and Driving Question Board Closure):
Learners compare their Lesson 1 prediction and Initial Model with what they now know, build a Final Explanation Poster (phenomenon, coordinate rule, mirror line, congruence proof) with the help of their Summary Tables, close the Driving Question Board and link the mathematics to road safety. The Final Explanation task assesses the same explanation in writing.

Lesson 1 — Symmetry All Around Us (Anchoring Phenomenon + Lines of Symmetry):
Learners observe the anchoring phenomenon (matatu mirror image) and supporting phenomena (maize leaf, Lake Victoria reflection). Working in pairs, they collect objects from the school environment (leaves, bottle caps, exercise book covers) and use a plane mirror to locate lines of symmetry. They record findings on a class Driving Question Board (DQB): "What makes the two halves match perfectly?" Formally, learners identify lines of symmetry in plane figures (equilateral triangle, rectangle, rhombus, regular hexagon) and distinguish between figures with one, many, or no lines of symmetry. Kenyan context: symmetry patterns in Maasai beadwork and kikoi fabric designs.

Lesson 2 — Properties of Reflection (Physical Investigation):
Learners use a plane mirror, tracing paper, and a drawn object (an arrow representing a matatu) to discover the four properties of reflection: (i) the image is the same size as the object; (ii) the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining each point to its image; (iii) the image is laterally inverted; (iv) object and image are equidistant from the mirror line. Groups fold tracing paper along the mirror line to verify coincidence. Learners update the DQB: "The mirror line is always in between — and at equal distances!" Connecting to the driving question: this explains why the lorry in the matatu mirror appears as far behind the glass as it truly is in front.

Lesson 3 — Drawing Images on a Plane Surface (Applying Properties):
Learners draw objects (a flag outline representing Kenya's flag shape) and given mirror lines on plain paper. Using the perpendicular bisector property established in Lesson 2, they construct the reflected image step by step — marking perpendiculars from key vertices, measuring equal distances, and connecting image points. Teacher emphasises accuracy with ruler and set square. Learners reflect irregular polygons and record: "Every point reflects to a unique image point across the mirror line." DQB updated with a student-drawn diagram showing object–mirror line–image.

Lesson 4 — Reflection on the Cartesian Plane (Mirror Lines x = k, y = k, y = x, y = −x):
Learners draw objects on a Cartesian grid and reflect them in horizontal (y = 0, y = k), vertical (x = 0, x = k), and diagonal (y = x, y = −x) mirror lines. Working in groups, they tabulate coordinate pairs of object and image vertices and identify the algebraic rule for each mirror line type. Connecting to the anchoring phenomenon: "The matatu mirror is like the y-axis — the image appears directly opposite." Learners practise at least three examples on squared paper and annotate coordinate transformations. DQB updated: "We can describe where the image lands using coordinates and algebra."

Lesson 5 — Finding the Equation of the Mirror Line:
Given an object and its image on the Cartesian plane, learners reverse-engineer the mirror line. They construct the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining corresponding vertices to locate the mirror line, then determine its equation (gradient and y-intercept). Problem contexts are Kenyan: a footpath reflected in a river (representing the Tana River valley), a road sign reflected in a puddle along Mombasa Road. Learners discover that the mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector locus and use the midpoint and gradient formulae to write its equation. DQB updated: "If we know the object and image, we can work backwards to find the mirror."

Lesson 6 — Introduction to Congruence and Direct vs. Opposite Congruence:
Learners make paper cutouts of triangles and quadrilaterals (connecting to chapati-cutter supporting phenomenon). They explore whether cutouts can be made to coincide by sliding and rotating only (direct/positive congruence) or whether flipping is needed (opposite/indirect congruence — the situation with the matatu mirror image). Learners classify pairs of shapes and record observations. The teacher introduces the formal definition of congruence: same shape, same size, all corresponding sides and angles equal. DQB updated: "Reflected images are always congruent to their objects — but they might be mirror images of each other!"

Lesson 7 — Congruence Tests for Triangles (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS):
Learners use different triangles (drawn on plain paper) to investigate the minimum conditions needed to guarantee two triangles are congruent. Working in groups, they attempt to construct non-congruent triangles given: (i) three sides — SSS; (ii) two sides and included angle — SAS; (iii) two angles and a side — AAS/SAA/ASA; (iv) right angle, hypotenuse and side — RHS. Groups present findings: each test yields exactly one triangle (up to congruence). Kenyan context: a carpenter in Gikomba market cutting identical triangular roof trusses — how many measurements are the minimum needed to guarantee all trusses are identical? DQB updated: "We only need THREE matching parts — but they must be the right three!"

Lesson 8 — Applications, Consolidation, and Model Revision:
Learners revisit the anchoring phenomenon fully: they now explain (using properties of reflection) why the lorry's mirror image is congruent to the actual lorry, why it appears laterally inverted, and which congruence test (SAS, using the mirror line as the axis of symmetry) proves the triangles formed by object–mirror line–image are congruent. Learners complete a group task: analysing driving mirror geometry (boda boda and matatu contexts) to justify NTSA road-safety guidance on mirror placement. A cumulative Cartesian model is produced — showing object, mirror line, image, perpendicular bisectors, labelled equations, and congruence annotations. DQB is reviewed: all initial questions are answered and remaining wonderings are noted for future strands. Formative assessment via class activity and a short written test.

This lesson is the seventh and penultimate lesson in the evidence-gathering sequence for Sub-Strand 2.2. In lessons 1–6, learners anchored their investigation in the matatu rear-view mirror phenomenon, discovered properties of reflection, plotted reflected images on the Cartesian plane, determined mirror line equations, and constructed reflected images on plain paper. What has remained unresolved — and explicitly tracked on the Driving Question Board — is the formal proof of why the mirror image is always an exact copy (same shape, same size) of the object. This lesson provides that proof through the four triangle congruence tests: SSS, SAS, AAS/ASA, and RHS.

Learners begin by predicting what minimum information about two triangles would be needed to be certain they are identical, connecting this to the matatu mirror context. They then carry out a hands-on investigation using paper cutouts of triangles, ruler, and compasses, attempting to construct a second triangle that matches a given one using only partial information (three sides; two sides and included angle; two angles and a side; right angle, hypotenuse and side). By comparing their constructions they observe that each test produces a unique triangle — sometimes a direct copy, sometimes a mirror-flipped copy — establishing the four congruence tests empirically before formalising them. In the explain phase learners apply these tests to a reflected triangle on the Cartesian plane to formally prove that a reflected image is always congruent (opposite/indirect congruence) to its object, directly answering the driving question.

The lesson is intentionally grounded in Kenya-relevant contexts throughout: the matatu mirror phenomenon drives every phase; triangular cutouts are labelled with Kenyan place-name vertices (e.g. triangle NMK for Nairobi–Mombasa–Kisumu); and learners discuss how congruence appears in everyday Kenyan life — identical triangular samosa pastry shapes cut from the same template, identical triangular roof trusses in Rift Valley buildings, and the tiling patterns on Nairobi pavements. By the end of the lesson learners can state all four congruence tests, apply them to verify that two triangles are congruent, and articulate why the matatu mirror image satisfies SSS — providing the formal mathematical resolution to the unit's anchoring phenomenon.

1. During the construction tasks (Observe Phase), did all learners correctly use the compass to mark off side lengths rather than estimating by eye? If not, what additional scaffolding on compass technique is needed before Lesson 8?
2. When learners wrote their formal congruence statements in the Explain Phase, did the majority use the correct vertex correspondence (e.g. △PQR ≅ △P'Q'R' rather than △PQR ≅ △Q'P'R')? If vertex order errors were common, how will I address this explicitly in the next lesson?
3. Did learners successfully distinguish between direct and opposite (indirect) congruence? Were they able to connect 'opposite congruence' back to the observed phenomenon of the lorry's headlights appearing reversed in the matatu mirror?
4. Looking at the green sticky notes on the DQB, how many groups produced a claim that both names the congruence test AND links it to the matatu mirror phenomenon? What does the proportion of such claims tell me about the depth of conceptual integration achieved?
5. Were the extension learners (SAS task) able to articulate why SAS also guarantees congruence — or did they simply accept it as a rule? How can I use their responses to deepen the whole class's understanding of why the minimum conditions are sufficient?

records.value:
This lesson is the third step in the evidence-gathering sequence for the matatu rear-view mirror phenomenon. In Lessons 1 and 2, learners identified lines of symmetry in plane figures and used physical mirrors and paper-folding to see that a fold line works as a mirror line. Lesson 3 now asks: can we capture what a mirror line does as precise coordinate rules? Learners will notice that each image point is as far from the mirror line as its object point and that the joining line meets it at a right angle; Lesson 4 tests and names these properties. Learners are given pre-drawn Cartesian grids and guided through reflecting a lorry-shaped polygon (a simple rectangle labelled to represent the Nairobi–Thika lorry) across four different mirror lines — the x-axis, the y-axis, y = x, and y = −x — recording how each vertex coordinate transforms.

The core sensemaking activity is a structured investigation in pairs: learners plot an object point, count grid squares perpendicularly to the mirror line, count the same distance on the other side, and record the new coordinates. After four reflections they compare their coordinate tables and articulate a rule for each mirror line (e.g., reflection in the y-axis maps (a, b) → (−a, b)). The lesson closes by returning to the phenomenon: because coordinates change in a predictable, rule-governed way, every length between any two vertices is preserved — exactly what makes the lorry image in the matatu mirror the same size as the real lorry.

By the end of the lesson learners will have generated a personal Reference Card of coordinate reflection rules, updated their Driving Question Board with new evidence, and revised their cumulative model to show mathematical notation alongside the mirror line and the 'congruent half' labels from Lesson 2. This sets up Lesson 5, where learners will determine the equation of an unknown mirror line given only the object and its image.

records.why: Step 2 told learners to touch a pencil to the mirror surface 'directly behind the image point'. The image is behind the mirror, where the paper is hidden by an ordinary mirror, so the step cannot be done. The standard school method is to draw sight-lines to the image and extend them behind the mirror; they cross at the image position (checked: each sight-line is the straight-line path from the eye to the virtual image, so two of them locate it). Marking only A' and B' keeps the time realistic; M' is found as a midpoint. This needs only a mirror, ruler and pencil.
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics, Chapter 25 Geometric Optics, 'Image Formation by Mirrors' (plane mirrors form virtual images; ray tracing to locate them); KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, 2.2 Reflection and Congruence (use a plane mirror to locate the image).

records.value: Each group of four receives a materials tray: one small plane mirror (held vertically using a lump of Blu-Tack), one A4 sheet with a bold arrow drawn on it (the 'matatu arrow' — tip labelled A, tail labelled B, a midpoint labelled M), a ruler, a set square, a sharp pencil, and a sheet of tracing paper. Step 1: Groups draw a straight horizontal mirror line across the middle of the paper, stand the mirror on it, and observe the image of the arrow in the mirror. Each learner sketches what they see and labels the image tip A', tail B', midpoint M'. Step 2: Groups mark the image points A' and B' with two sight-lines (the teacher demonstrates: with the mirror upright on the mirror line, look at the image of A and lay a ruler on the paper so that the ruler and its reflection form one straight line pointing at the image of A; draw a thin line along the ruler up to the mirror line; repeat from a different position; then continue both lines behind the mirror line with dotted lines. A' is where the two dotted lines cross. Repeat for B'. Where a clear plastic or glass sheet is available it can replace the mirror, and the image points can be marked directly behind it. M' is the midpoint of A'B'). Step 3: Groups remove the mirror, join A to A', B to B', and M to M' with straight lines. Step 4: Using a ruler, groups measure (i) the distance from A to the mirror line, and the distance from A' to the mirror line; (ii) same for B and B'; (iii) same for M and M'. Groups record all six measurements in a results table. Step 5: Using a set square, groups check whether each connecting segment (AA', BB', MM') is perpendicular to the mirror line and record 'Yes' or 'No.'

Four tasks could not be finished in 12 minutes, so pairs now do A, B and one of C or D.

The anchoring phenomenon says the lorry's right headlight 'appears on the left in the mirror'. For a driver looking in a rear-view mirror, the lorry's right headlight actually appears on the driver's right, the same side as in real life; the 'flip' is front-to-back (the image seems to face the driver), and left-right swapping only appears if you compare the image with the lorry seen face to face. The statement is therefore misleading as written, although the wording 'lateral inversion' is standard in Kenyan textbooks. Suggested: keep the matatu mirror phenomenon but use a clearer example of lateral inversion such as the word AMBULANCE written reversed on the front of an ambulance so it reads correctly in a driver's mirror, or the letter F in a mirror (Lesson 1), and say that the image faces the opposite way along the line of sight. Teachers must decide whether to change the phenomenon wording.

value.purpose: Learners use paper cut-outs to discover that two shapes can be congruent (same shape and same size) in two different ways: direct congruence, where one shape fits exactly on the other by sliding or turning it, and opposite congruence, where one shape must be flipped over first, like a mirror image. They also extend lines of symmetry to planes of symmetry in solid objects.
value.knowledge:
• Describe congruent shapes as shapes with the same shape and the same size.
• Distinguish direct congruence (one shape fits on the other by sliding and/or turning, with no flip) from opposite congruence (one shape must be flipped over to fit).
• Recognise that a shape with a line of symmetry fits both ways, so its flipped copy also fits without a flip.
• Describe a plane of symmetry as a plane that cuts a solid into two mirror-image halves.
value.skills:
• Make pairs of identical shapes by cutting folded paper and test them by sliding, turning and flipping.
• Classify pairs of congruent shapes as direct or opposite and record the evidence in a table.
• Find planes of symmetry of a box-shaped object from the immediate environment.
value.attitudes:
• Show respect by recognising the input of every member of the group when making and testing the cut-outs.

records.value:
This lesson uses the time freed by combining the two lines-of-symmetry lessons. It covers the KICD learning experience in which learners work in a group and make paper cut-outs of different identical shapes to identify direct and opposite congruent shapes, and it adds planes of symmetry for solid objects.

In the Predict phase learners look at a photograph (or teacher sketch) of the hills of Homa Bay reflected in still water on Lake Victoria near Kisumu and predict whether the reflection is an exact copy of the hills and whether a copy of the hills could be slid or turned on the desk to land on the reflection. In the Observe phase, groups fold a sheet of paper, draw a shape that has no line of symmetry (for example a lopsided letter F or an irregular quadrilateral) and cut through both layers to get two identical shapes. They test them: one piece fits exactly on the other by sliding and turning, but when one piece is flipped over it becomes a mirror copy and no longer fits without flipping it back. They then repeat with a shape that has a line of symmetry and with a circle cut-out like a chapati cutter, and find that the flip makes no difference for those shapes.

In the Explain phase the class names the two kinds of congruence (direct and opposite), links opposite congruence to what a mirror does, and extends lines of symmetry to planes of symmetry using a box-shaped object. The lesson closes by updating the Driving Question Board and the unit model. The formal tests for congruent triangles come in Lesson 7.

Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 5 min, Observe 14 min (hand out materials 1 min, then the three tasks of 7, 4 and 2 min), Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 5 min, Model Building 6 min. If time runs short, drop the plane-of-symmetry discussion to one minute and read only three sticky notes aloud.
records.old:
This lesson places learners in the role of mathematical investigators, using the anchoring phenomenon — the matatu rear-view mirror on the Nairobi–Thika highway — as the motivating puzzle. In Lesson 1, learners established that the mirror image of the lorry appears identical in size and shape to the real lorry. Lesson 2 now asks: what is the special line that makes the two halves match so perfectly? Working in pairs, learners collect objects from the school environment (maize leaves, bottle caps, exercise book covers) and use a small plane mirror to search for lines of symmetry, physically observing that placing the mirror along a line of symmetry produces an image that completes the original figure seamlessly — exactly what the matatu conductor's mirror does for the driver on the highway.

In the Observe and Explain phases, learners move from informal object exploration to formal geometric figures. They fold cut-out shapes — equilateral triangle, rectangle, rhombus, and regular hexagon — to find and draw every line of symmetry, then record results in a class table. The Kenyan cultural context is woven in: learners examine photographs of Maasai beadwork collars and kikoi fabric strips and identify how the symmetry patterns are constructed, connecting abstract mathematics to the textiles of their own communities.

By the end of the lesson, learners can state, in their own words, that a line of symmetry is a mirror line — the same kind of line that separates the lorry from its image in the matatu mirror. This precise language anchors the Driving Question Board update and advances the unit's central argument: that reflection along a mirror line preserves shape and size, which is the foundation of congruence.

Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 5 min, Observe 15 min (hand out materials 1 min, then the three activities of 4, 7 and 3 min), Explain 9 min, Driving Question Board 5 min, Model Building 6 min.

Before I tell you anything, I want your predictions.' Write the three questions on the board. Allow 2 minutes of silent writing [WAIT TIME: 2 minutes]. Then say: 'Compare with your partner for one minute.' Cold-call 3 pairs (one that says the reflection is an exact copy, one that says it is different, and one that mentions flipping). After each response wait 10 seconds before moving on. Record key phrases on the board under the heading 'Tunafikiria / We think...' Do NOT say which predictions are right.
value.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Justification: committing to a prediction about sliding, turning and flipping before handling any shapes makes learners' ideas about 'same shape and size' visible and gives them something to test in the Observe phase.
value.formativeAssessment: Listen for whether learners distinguish SIZE and SHAPE (the same) from POSITION and DIRECTION (different). Note learners who say 'the reflection is the same, so I can just slide it' (a direct-congruence idea) and learners who mention 'upside down' or 'flipped' (an opposite-congruence idea). Flag one of each to share in the Explain phase.

value.learnerExperience: Groups of four receive scrap paper, scissors, pencils and a ruler. Task 1 (7 min): Each group folds a sheet of paper in half, draws on the folded sheet a shape with NO line of symmetry (for example a lopsided letter F or an irregular quadrilateral), and cuts through both layers to get two identical pieces. Learners draw a small dot in pencil on the upper face of each piece. They test: (a) with both dots facing up, can piece B be made to land exactly on piece A by sliding and/or turning it on the desk? (b) Now turn piece B over (dot face down): can it land exactly on piece A without being turned back over? Task 2 (4 min): Groups repeat the test with a shape that HAS a line of symmetry (an isosceles triangle or a rectangle) and with a circle cut-out (like the circular cutter a cook uses to cut chapati). Task 3 (2 min): Each learner records results in a table with columns: Shape | Has a line of symmetry? | Fits by sliding or turning only? | Fits when one piece is flipped over?
value.teacherMoves: Distribute the materials (1 minute). Say: 'A cook in a Nairobi restaurant cuts every chapati with the same circular cutter, so every chapati is exactly the same shape and size. Today we test what it takes for two pieces to match.' Demonstrate ONE cut-through-two-layers on the board so the method is clear, but do not show the test results. Set a visible 7-minute timer for Task 1. Circulate. When a group says the flipped piece 'does not fit', ask: 'What can you do to the piece to make it fit again?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] When a group says both pieces always fit for their shape, ask them to check that their shape really has no line of symmetry by folding it. At the end of Task 1 ask: 'Hands up if piece B fitted on piece A when both dots were up.' Then: 'Hands up if it still fitted after you turned it over.' Give the 4-minute Task 2 and then 2 minutes for recording. Cold-call 4 groups to report one row each.
value.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete Manipulative Exploration with Contrasting Cases: handling a shape that has no line of symmetry beside one that has one lets learners find, from their own evidence, that flipping matters only for some shapes. The table turns the physical actions into recorded evidence.
value.formativeAssessment: Check tables for: (a) lopsided shape: fits by sliding/turning (yes), fits after a flip (no, unless flipped back); (b) shape with a line of symmetry: fits both ways; (c) circle: fits both ways. Look for learners who confuse turning (rotating) with flipping; ask them to show with the dot: 'Is the dot still on top?' Note groups that explain WHY the symmetric shapes fit both ways (the flipped copy looks the same as the original), as they are ready for the lines-of-symmetry link in the Explain phase.

value.learnerExperience: Groups report their evidence and the class builds two statements: DIRECT congruence means the two shapes have the same shape and size and one fits on the other by sliding and/or turning only; OPPOSITE congruence means the two shapes have the same shape and size but one is a mirror copy of the other, so it must be flipped over to fit. Learners copy these statements and then classify three pairs shown on the board: (i) two identical lopsided triangles in the same orientation, (ii) the same triangle and its mirror image, (iii) two circles of the same radius. Next, for 3 minutes, learners find planes of symmetry: the teacher holds up a box-shaped object (for example a matchbox or a brick-shaped box with three different edge lengths) and a card 'plane'; learners say where a flat cut would divide the box into two mirror-image halves and how many such cuts exist.
value.teacherMoves: Cold-call 3 groups for their evidence and write the two definitions on the board after the third response, asking learners to underline 'same shape and size' in both. Say: 'In the Lake Victoria picture, which kind of copy is the reflection?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Confirm: 'It is a mirror copy, so we expect OPPOSITE congruence. We will check this properly when we measure mirror images in Lesson 4 and prove it for triangles in Lesson 7.' Then show the three pairs on the board and ask each time: 'Direct, opposite, or both? What is your evidence?' [WAIT 10 seconds each; accept 'both' for the circles and explain that a shape with a line of symmetry looks the same when flipped.] Then say: 'A line of symmetry works in a flat shape. value.observed: Learners observed that two identical paper cut-outs of a shape with no line of symmetry fit exactly on each other by sliding or turning, but when one piece is flipped over it no longer fits unless flipped back. value.learned: Two shapes are congruent when they have the same shape and the same size. Direct congruence: one shape fits on the other by sliding and/or turning only. Opposite congruence: one shape is a mirror copy of the other and must be flipped over to fit. A shape with a line of symmetry fits both ways. A plane of symmetry cuts a solid into two mirror-image halves; a box with three different edge lengths has 3 planes of symmetry.
value.explained: The reflection of the hills in Lake Victoria, and the image of the lorry in the matatu mirror, are mirror copies, so we expect them to be opposite congruent to their objects: the same shape and size, but flipped. This is a hypothesis for now. It will be tested by measuring in Lesson 4 and proved for triangles in Lesson 7.

The KICD rubric has no indicator for congruence tests. records.value: Diagram: the mirror line is drawn as a straight line. The object (lorry) is on one side and the image is on the opposite side. Dotted lines join corresponding points such as the right headlight and its image. Each dotted line meets the mirror line at 90 degrees with equal marked distances on each side. (a) Property II: the object and image are equidistant from the mirror line, so the image looks as far behind the glass as the lorry is in front of it. (b) Property I: the image is the same size as the object, because reflection does not stretch or shrink any length. We confirmed this when the tracing-paper fold along the mirror line made the object and image coincide exactly. (c) Property IV: the image is laterally inverted, so left and right are reversed in the image. The word AMBULANCE is painted reversed on the ambulance; the mirror reverses it again, so the driver reads it correctly. This is a reversal of left and right, not a change of size or shape. The mirror line is also the perpendicular bisector of every segment joining an object point to its image point (Property III), so the position of the image is completely predictable. (d) A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines of symmetry (one joining the midpoints of each pair of opposite sides), an equilateral triangle has 3 (each from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side), and the letter F has 0. (e) In the line x = 0, (a, b) maps to (-a, b): A'(-1, 1), B'(-4, 1), C'(-4, 3). In the line y = x, (a, b) maps to (b, a): A'(1, 1), B'(1, 4), C'(3, 4). Each image vertex is plotted the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as its object vertex, on the opposite side, and the image vertices are joined in order.
